options.text: The remnant left after a supernova
A vast cloud of gas (mainly hydrogen) and dust from which stars form
A type of galaxy
A dying star that has run out of fuel

questions.explanation: A nebula is a vast cloud of gas (mainly hydrogen) and dust in space. Gravity causes regions within a nebula to collapse, eventually forming protostars and then stars.

questions.stem: What keeps a main sequence star stable?

options.text: The balance between outward radiation pressure from fusion and inward gravitational force
The star's magnetic field preventing expansion
The constant supply of fuel from nearby nebulae
The absence of any nuclear reactions

questions.explanation: A main sequence star is in equilibrium because the outward radiation pressure from nuclear fusion in its core exactly balances the inward gravitational force. If either dominates, the star expands or contracts.

questions.stem: What is the correct life cycle for a low-mass star like our Sun?

options.text: Protostar, nebula, main sequence, supernova, neutron star
Nebula, protostar, main sequence, red giant, planetary nebula, white dwarf
Nebula, protostar, main sequence, white dwarf, red giant
Nebula, protostar, main sequence, red supergiant, supernova, black hole

questions.explanation: A low-mass star like the Sun follows this path: nebula, protostar, main sequence, red giant, planetary nebula, and finally white dwarf. It does not have enough mass to end in a supernova.

questions.stem: Why do massive stars have shorter lifetimes than smaller stars?

options.text: They lose mass through solar wind
They have less hydrogen fuel
They are further from other stars
Their higher core temperatures cause them to burn through fuel much faster

questions.explanation: Although massive stars have more fuel, their much higher core temperatures cause fusion to occur at a far greater rate. They consume their fuel much more quickly, giving them lifetimes of only millions of years compared to billions for Sun-like stars.

questions.stem: What triggers a supernova in a massive star?

options.text: The outer layers become too cold and fall inward
The star absorbs too much light from nearby stars
The star collides with another star
Iron accumulates in the core and its fusion absorbs energy, so the core can no longer support itself and collapses

questions.explanation: When a massive star fuses elements up to iron, iron fusion absorbs energy rather than releasing it. The core can no longer support itself against gravity, collapses catastrophically in less than a second, and triggers a supernova explosion.

questions.stem: Where do elements heavier than iron (such as gold and silver) come from?

options.text: They form when white dwarfs cool down
They were all created during the Big Bang
They are created in supernova explosions
They are formed inside main sequence stars

questions.explanation: Elements heavier than iron can only be created in the extreme temperatures and pressures of supernova explosions. These elements are then scattered into space and may become part of new stars, planets, and even living organisms.

questions.stem: What are the two possible remnants left behind after a supernova?

options.text: Neutron star or black hole
Protostar or main sequence star
White dwarf or red giant
Planetary nebula or red dwarf

questions.explanation: After a supernova, the collapsed core remains as either a neutron star (if the remnant is 1.4-3 solar masses) or a black hole (if the remnant exceeds about 3 solar masses). Which one forms depends on the mass of the remaining core.
